models.approach: Argue from the platforms' own behaviour: they already curate, so they already publish.
plan: Introduction: rephrase the immunity claim, then agree with a limit.
Body 1: curation makes them publishers, not noticeboards.
Body 2: concede the censorship risk, then answer it with a narrow duty.
Conclusion: restate, and say what liability would actually change.

paras.text: Social networks have long insisted that they are neutral pipes carrying whatever the public pours into them. [[I would argue]] that this description stopped being accurate years ago, and I agree that platforms should bear legal responsibility for the falsehoods they distribute, although not for every one of them.

[[The key issue is]] that these companies do not merely host content, they rank it. An algorithm that decides which of a million posts a user sees is making an editorial judgement, and it makes that judgement in favour of whatever holds attention, which is [[invariably|Invariable]] the most inflammatory version of any claim. A newspaper is liable for what it prints because it chose to print it; the choice here is identical, only automated.

[[Admittedly]], unlimited liability would be dangerous. A company facing ruin for a single post would delete anything contested, and legitimate argument would be the first casualty, so the fear of over-removal is not [[frivolous]]. [[Nevertheless]], the remedy is a narrow duty rather than none: responsibility for material the platform actively promoted, and for anything it was told about and left up.

[[In conclusion]], I agree that legal responsibility should follow the editorial power these firms already exercise. Liability of that shape would not silence users; it would simply make amplification something a company must [[substantiate]], which is what every other publisher has always had to do.

notes: The essay agrees but narrows the claim in the first paragraph, which lets it survive the obvious objection instead of ignoring it.
The newspaper comparison does the argumentative work. One analogy, developed in two sentences, is worth more than three assertions.
The concession is answered with a specific legal test, promoted or notified, rather than with reassurance.

models.approach: Defend the immunity on practical grounds: scale, and who ends up deciding what is true.
plan: Introduction: the aim is right, the instrument is wrong.
Body 1: the volume argument, with numbers.
Body 2: who decides truth, plus a concession about clear-cut harms.

paras.text: Nobody defends the spread of falsehood online, but the wish to punish somebody for it should not decide the law. [[In my opinion]] making platforms liable for what their users write would be a serious mistake, however [[compelling]] the motive behind it.

[[First and foremost]], the volume makes the duty impossible to discharge honestly. Several hundred hours of video arrive on the largest platforms every minute, and no combination of moderators and software can [[ascertain]] the truth of that in real time. Faced with liability, a rational company does not verify; it deletes on suspicion, and the safest thing to delete is anything unusual, unpopular or new.

[[More importantly|Importantly]], such a law hands the definition of truth to whoever is in office. Claims about the origins of a virus or the conduct of a war have moved from forbidden to accepted within two years, and a statute written in the first year would have suppressed the second. [[Granted]], deliberate medical hoaxes and incitement are different: those are already illegal, and enforcing existing law against the authors is entirely [[germane]].

[[All things considered]], I disagree with the proposal while accepting the problem. Transparency about what algorithms promote, real penalties for coordinated deception, and rapid access to correction would each [[ameliorate]] the harm without asking a company to become a court.

notes: Agreeing with the motive and rejecting the mechanism is the most persuasive way to disagree. It removes the suspicion that you simply do not care about the problem.
The two objections are different in kind, practical then constitutional, which stops body two repeating body one.
Three alternatives in the conclusion turn a refusal into a proposal.

models.approach: Distinguish hosting from amplifying, and put liability only on the second.
plan: Introduction: the question is too broad as posed; split it.
Body 1: no liability for what is merely hosted, and why.
Body 2: liability for what is promoted, and why that is different.
Conclusion: the line, and how it could be enforced.

paras.text: The proposal treats a platform as a single thing, when in practice it performs two very different jobs: it stores what users write, and it decides what users see. [[To a certain extent]] I agree with legal responsibility, but only for the second of these.

Holding a company liable for mere storage would be [[incongruous]]. A telephone company is not prosecuted for a lie told down its line, and the volume of material makes prior inspection [[hypothetical]] rather than practical. Such a rule would also [[dissuade]] anybody from starting a competitor, since only the largest firms could afford the moderation, and the result would be an even narrower [[hegemony]] than the one we have.

[[By contrast]], promotion is a decision, and decisions attract responsibility. When a system calculates that a fabricated claim will hold attention and pushes it to two million feeds, the company has done something no telephone line does. [[It is evident that]] the harm comes from the reach rather than the existence: an untrue post nobody sees injures nobody, and the reach was chosen by the platform.

[[On balance]], then, responsibility should attach to amplification alone. The line is workable, since every platform already logs what it promoted and to whom, and applying [[scrutiny]] there would change behaviour without turning the internet's storage into somebody's liability.

notes: Splitting the subject of the question, here hosting against amplifying, is the most reliable way to write a partial agreement that still argues something.
The telephone comparison is used and then explicitly limited in body two. An analogy you police yourself is stronger than one you leave open.
The conclusion answers how, not just what. Saying the platforms already keep these logs makes the proposal look practical rather than clever.
